parts.label: (a)

markscheme_points.text: angle (subtended at centre of circle) when arc length = radius

hints: Hint 1: Think about how an angle at the centre of a circle is linked to the length of the curved arc it cuts off compared to the size of the circle itself.
parts.proper_answer: The radian is the angle subtended at the centre of a circle by an arc of length equal to the radius of the circle.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **What a radian really means**
Think of the centre of a circle with two lines going out to the edge. They cut off a short curved piece of circumference. If you make that curved piece exactly as long as the radius, the angle between the two lines is 1 radian. So a radian links arc length $s$ and radius $r$ very simply, with $\theta = s/r$ when $\theta$ is in radians.

parts.label: (b)
hints: Hint 1: Start by picturing one full turn of the minute hand. How many radians is a full circle, and how many seconds does this hand take for that turn?
Hint 2: Now divide the total angle for one revolution by the total time in seconds to get angular speed in $\text{rad s}^{-1}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Linking revolutions to radians and seconds**
One full revolution is an angle of $2\pi$ radians. The minute hand takes one hour for this, so the period is $$T = 1.0 \times 60 \times 60 = 3600 \text{ s}$$ You have total angle and total time, so angular speed is angle per unit time.

Step 2: **Calculating omega**
Use: $$\omega = \frac{\theta}{T} = \frac{2\pi}{T}$$ Then: $$\omega = \frac{2\pi}{3600} = 1.7 \times 10^{-3} \text{ rad s}^{-1}$$ This tiny value makes sense because a clock hand turns very slowly.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.part_stem: During a time interval of $1400\text{ s}$, the centre of gravity of the piece of modelling clay in Fig. 1.1 moves through a total distance of $0.44\text{ m}$.
parts.text: Calculate the angle through which the minute hand moves in this time interval.
hints: Hint 1: You already know how fast the angle changes each second from part (b). Think how to scale that up to 1400 s of steady turning.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **From speed to angle**
With constant angular speed, angle grown is simply speed multiplied by time: $$\theta = \omega t$$ Using $\omega = 1.745 \times 10^{-3} \text{ rad s}^{-1}$ and $t = 1400 \text{ s}$: $$\theta = 1.745 \times 10^{-3} \times 1400 = 2.4 \text{ rad}$$ That is less than $2\pi$, so less than half a revolution, as expected for 1400 s compared to 3600 s.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: Picture the clay moving along a circular arc of radius L. You know the distance travelled along the arc and the angle turned through - how are arc length, radius and angle connected?
Hint 2: Rearrange that arc-length relation to make L the subject and substitute $s = 0.44 \text{ m}$ and your angle from (c)(i).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Seeing L as the radius of the arc**
The clay moves on a circle of radius $L$. The distance it travels is an arc length $s = 0.44 \text{ m}$ corresponding to angle $\theta \approx 2.44 \text{ rad}$.

Step 2: **Finding L**
For angles in radians: $$s = L\theta$$ so $$L = \frac{s}{\theta} = \frac{0.44}{2.44} = 0.18 \text{ m}$$ This is a sensible length for a clock minute hand.

parts.label: (c)(iii)
parts.text: Calculate the magnitude of the centripetal acceleration of the piece of modelling clay.
hints: Hint 1: Recall that even at constant speed, circular motion needs an inward acceleration. Which quantities - radius and angular speed - control how large it is?
Hint 2: Use $a = r\omega^2$ with $r = L$ from (c)(ii) and $\omega$ from (b), keeping $\omega$ in $\text{rad s}^{-1}$.
parts.proper_answer: $a = L\omega^2 = 0.18 \times (1.74 \times 10^{-3})^2 = 5.5 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m s}^{-2}$ towards the centre.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Choosing the centripetal formula**
For uniform circular motion the acceleration is always towards the centre with magnitude: $$a = r\omega^2$$ Here $r = L$. The $\omega^2$ tells you that a very small $\omega$ gives an extremely small $a$.

Step 2: **Substituting values**
$$a = 0.18 \times (1.745 \times 10^{-3})^2$$ $$a = 5.5 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m s}^{-2}$$ The direction is towards the fixed end of the hand. The value is tiny because the clock turns so slowly.

parts.label: (d)
parts.text: Use your answer in (c)(iii) to explain why the variation with time of the magnitude of the force exerted by the minute hand on the piece of modelling clay is negligible as the minute hand undergoes one full revolution.

markscheme_points.text: centripetal acceleration is negligible compared with acceleration of free fall or numerical comparison establishing answer to (c)(iii) << 9.81
resultant force is negligible compared with weight (of modelling clay) (so variation is negligible) or force exerted by minute hand (approximately) equal (and opposite) to weight of modelling clay

hints: Hint 1: Compare the size of your acceleration in (c)(iii) with the familiar acceleration due to gravity $g \approx 9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2}$. What does that tell you about the extra force needed for circular motion?

Hint 2: Think about the two forces on the clay - its weight $mg$ downwards and the contact force from the hand. If $ma$ is tiny compared to $mg$, how much does the hand force need to change as direction changes?
parts.proper_answer: Centripetal acceleration $5.5 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m s}^{-2}$ is negligible compared with $g = 9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2}$. Hence the centripetal force $ma$ is negligible compared with the weight $mg$, so the force from the hand is approximately equal and opposite to the weight at all times with negligible variation.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Comparing accelerations**
Your value $a \approx 5 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m s}^{-2}$ is about 10 million times smaller than $g = 9.81 \text{ m s}^{-2}$. Since force is $m$ times acceleration, the inward force $ma$ needed for circular motion is negligible next to the weight $mg$.

Step 2: **Why the hand force hardly changes**
The clay has weight $mg$ downwards plus the force from the hand. The vector sum must equal the tiny $ma$ towards the centre. Because $ma$ is so small, the hand must supply a force almost exactly balancing the weight at every position. As the hand rotates, the direction of $ma$ rotates, but its size is so tiny that the change in the magnitude of the hand force is negligible.
